reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: Shohei Ohtani is the only player in baseball you have to evaluate twice, and both evaluations come back elite. As a hitter, the contact quality is genuinely absurd — xwOBA at .409 (98th percentile), xSLG at .557 (98th percentile), 15.9% barrels (95th) — and a 15.1% walk rate (96th) means he's manufacturing traffic even when pitchers try to dance around him. The swing-and-miss (28.4% whiff rate, 29th percentile) is the one real friction point in an otherwise historic bat profile, and it's the reason ValuCast's projection of .281/.395/.541 with 38 home runs carries medium confidence rather than a stamp of certainty. On the mound, a 2.69 xERA and 30.4% whiff rate as a pitcher put him in the conversation with the best starters in the league — the chase rate (30.0%, 47th percentile) suggests hitters can lay off his stuff when they're disciplined, but a 98.1 mph fastball (94th percentile) at 2486 rpm (89th) makes that easier said than done.

reports.name: Bobby Witt Jr.
reports.published_report: Bobby Witt Jr. is the rare shortstop who can beat you four different ways — he hits for average, hits for power, walks enough to keep pitchers honest, and runs whenever he wants. The Statcast profile backs every bit of it: xBA at the 100th percentile, xwOBA at .392 (96th), average exit velocity at 93.3 mph (95th), and a 30.3 ft/s sprint speed that puts him in the 99th percentile for speed. The one real question is the chase rate — 32.8% sits in just the 31st percentile — but with a 16.9% strikeout rate, he's handling the contact side well enough that it hasn't become a liability. ValuCast projects .291/.359/.487 with 25 home runs and 47 steals across 677 plate appearances, and at 25 years old, that's not a ceiling — that's the floor of what this player already is.

reports.name: James Wood
reports.published_report: James Wood is a true middle-of-the-order force at 23 — the kind of hitter whose contact quality is genuinely elite, not just above-average. His 95.3 mph average exit velocity, 22.6% barrel rate, and 60.2% hard-hit rate all sit at the 100th percentile; the .420 xwOBA and .597 xSLG aren't projections inflated by luck, they're the natural output of that much raw damage. The one honest tension in his profile is the 30.0% strikeout rate (11th percentile) running alongside a 15.9% walk rate (98th percentile) — he draws walks at an elite clip because pitchers know better than to give him anything to hit, but he still whiffs on the pitches that aren't strikes, so the K number is real and isn't going away. ValuCast's projection — .263/.378/.507 with 37 home runs and 22 steals over 732 plate appearances — reflects a player whose underlying contact quality is so far ahead of his batting average that the slash line almost undersells him.

reports.name: Nick Kurtz
reports.published_report: Nick Kurtz is a 23-year-old masher with elite contact quality and a genuinely elite eye — the kind of combination that makes strikeout rate a secondary concern. His 94.5 mph average exit velocity, 19.0% barrel rate, and 59.0% hard-hit rate all sit at the 98th percentile, and his 19.3% walk rate is off the charts; the one real blemish is a 36.2% whiff rate that lands at the 4th percentile, which is why his xBA (.260) lags well behind his .394 xwOBA (96th percentile) — he's doing enormous damage on contact, but he misses a lot of pitches he doesn't chase. ValuCast's current projection has him at .273/.405/.524 with 38 home runs over 707 plate appearances, and the walk rate alone is enough to prop up the OBP even if the strikeouts don't come down much. The whiff rate is the thing to watch; if pitchers find a consistent way to exploit it, the batting average could slide, but the power and patience floor here is genuinely high.

reports.name: Paul Skenes
reports.published_report: Paul Skenes is the real thing — a 23-year-old who already sits in the 93rd percentile in both xERA (2.76) and xwOBA (.260) against big-league hitters, backed by a 30.1% strikeout rate at the 93rd percentile and a walk rate of just 5.6%. The profile tells you why: elite stuff and elite command is a rare combination, and the contact quality numbers — 6.5% barrel rate, 88.1 mph average exit velo — confirm hitters aren't squaring him up even when they make contact. ValuCast projects 182.6 innings of 3.30 ERA ball with 224 strikeouts and a 1.04 WHIP, which is ace production, and the Statcast floor makes that projection feel conservative rather than optimistic. The one thing to watch is that whiff rate (28.3%, 73rd percentile) and chase rate (33.1%, 75th percentile) are good but not elite — his dominance is built more on stuff quality and location than pure swing-and-miss vapor, which is a sustainable foundation, not a flaw.

reports.name: Logan Webb
reports.published_report: Webb is the rare pitcher who wins without overpowering anyone — 92.5 mph fastball, 20.3% whiff rate, and nobody in the league cares because he gets 33.4% chase and barrels just 5.8% of what he serves up. The Statcast profile tells the whole story: his walk rate (6.3% BB%, 81st percentile) and barrel suppression do the heavy lifting that strikeouts can't, and the contact he does allow stays manageable — 89.7 mph average exit velo doesn't scare you. ValuCast projects a 3.53 ERA over 184 innings, which sits a tick better than his 3.96 xERA suggests, though the gap isn't alarming given how consistently he pitches to contact on his terms. The one real ceiling cap is that 37th-percentile strikeout rate — he's not punching through a lineup a third time on stuff alone, so if his command or chase numbers slip, there's no swing-and-miss floor to bail him out.

reports.name: Colt Emerson
reports.peak_summary: Projection: low-end everyday regular with medium risk. The current bat shape is mixed over 169 PA.
reports.published_report: Colt Emerson is a 20-year-old shortstop holding his own in AAA, and the most interesting thing about his game right now is that the power is real while the approach is still catching up. His .214 ISO at AAA (translating to .160 at the MLB level) isn't a fluke of a hitter's park or a hot week — it's the carrying tool, and it's why his .816 OPS reads as believable rather than inflated. The problem is the strikeout rate: 27% at AAA translates to roughly 25.4% against big-league pitching, above the 22.0% MLB average, and his walk rate doesn't do enough to offset it — 10% in the minors softens to about 8.9% in translation, barely a tick above league average. The projection sees a bench or platoon outcome as the most likely landing spot right now, with the ceiling a low-end everyday regular if the hit tool firms up and the approach matures — which, at 20, isn't an unreasonable ask.

The problem is the free pass never shows up: a 4.5% BB% against a 41.4% chase rate (4th percentile) means pitchers have a clear road map, and until that changes, his .315 OBP will stay the ceiling on his value even as the power projects to 27 home runs with a .514 SLG. He wins by hitting the ball hard enough often enough that the swing decisions don't kill him — but he's one extended slump away from reminding you why plate discipline matters.

reports.name: Shane McClanahan

That contact quality problem is the whole story: his xERA of 4.27 and .320 xwOBA say the performance is closer to league-average than the 3.37 ERA ValuCast projects him to post, which is why this read carries medium confidence. The projection is essentially a bet that the swing-and-miss (61st percentile whiff rate) and chase numbers hold up enough to outrun the damage when contact does land — a reasonable bet for a pitcher returning from injury, but not a sure one.

The 7.1% walk rate is genuinely good (73rd percentile), but hitters are barely chasing at 26.9% (16th percentile), his K% sits at 20.2% (35th percentile), and the contact he does allow is hard: 42.8% hard-hit rate (22nd percentile), 9.2% barrel rate (27th percentile). ValuCast projects a 3.91 ERA over 184.6 innings, but a 4.51 xERA against that projection is a real gap worth naming — he's been getting results the underlying contact numbers don't fully support. The one thing that decides his outcome is whether he can generate more swing-and-miss; without it, a back-end starter who gets by on command is one cold stretch from the ERA catching up to the xERA.

reports.name: Emerson Hancock
reports.published_report: Emerson Hancock is a strike-thrower who doesn't miss enough bats — and that gap is the whole story. His 6.1% walk rate puts him in the 84th percentile for command, but a 25.4% chase rate (7th percentile) and 22.9% whiff rate (33rd percentile) mean hitters aren't expanding the zone or losing the ball, which is why his xERA sits at 4.48 despite the clean walk numbers. The 44.9% hard-hit rate (12th percentile) is the natural consequence — guys are making contact and squaring it up. ValuCast's projection of a 3.78 ERA over 154.83 innings reflects some optimism that his 95.4 mph fastball with 2374 rpm spin (76th percentile) can play better than the swing-and-miss numbers currently suggest, but the path there runs straight through whether he can develop a swing-and-miss offering — because right now, the walk prevention alone isn't enough to carry a rotation spot.

reports.name: Juan Brito
reports.peak_summary: Projection: bench or platoon bat with low risk. The current bat shape is mixed over 287 PA.
reports.published_report:
Juan Brito is a 24-year-old second baseman who wins with his approach, not his bat. At AAA this season, he's walking at a 15% clip in 287 PA — translating to an 11.8% MLB-equivalent BB% against a league average of 8.5% — while his 17% strikeout rate lands him in the 85th percentile among his peer pool. That's a legitimately elite contact-and-patience combination for a middle infielder.

The honest catch: the power isn't there yet. A .146 ISO at AAA projects to .130 in the majors, where the average is .150, and the .393 SLG that looks passable in the minors gets thin real fast at the next level. The projection sees a bench or platoon bat, with more upside than today's production shows — and Brito is moving up +1.9 in ValuCast's rankings over the past three days. His floor is real, his ceiling depends entirely on whether the power develops enough to punish pitchers who find his zone.

reports.published_report: Milan Tolentino is a left-handed shortstop with a real power tool and a strikeout problem that's going to define his ceiling. In 277 PA at AAA this season, he's posting a .459 SLG with a .211 ISO — the pop translates; his MiLB-equivalent ISO of .161 still clears the MLB average — but a 32% K rate in the minors becomes a projected 29.2% against big-league pitching, and that's a hard number to build a lineup role around. The approach (12% BB at AAA, ~9.8% equivalent) is functional but not enough to compensate, and the .248 AVG sitting against a .342 BABIP tells you the contact quality isn't bailing him out. ValuCast projects him as a bench or platoon bat — the power is genuine, but until that strikeout rate bends, everyday at-bats are a stretch.

The ValuCast projection (.262/.347/.453, 24 HR in 593 PA) reflects exactly that: a patient, above-average offensive player whose value comes from the walk rate (11.0%, 69th percentile) and on-base consistency, not from carrying a lineup with raw power.
